For a strictly exterior contact translated to zero, the direction of a nearest point of K gives t at least its positive distance from zero. Compactness gives a finite b and a uniform bound on the other coordinates. The derivative of (t,s)→(t,ts) has diagonal blocks 1 and tI, so the Jacobian is t^(d−1). Integrating in t yields the exact pushforward with total volume |K|. The range t∈[a,b] gives bounded density and bounded projection. Reverse Fatou with the common upper envelope t^(d−1) on [a,b] gives upper semicontinuity.

With representatives at t₀,t₁>0, divide weights λ/t₀ and (1−λ)/t₁ by their sum. The resulting height is the reciprocal of that sum and the projected point is λs₀+(1−λ)s₁. The image is compact and convex, and projection of int K is open by the homeomorphism (t,s)→(t,ts) on t>0. For s in the image interior distinct from s₀, extend the segment through s and apply the positive-weight lift with an interior representative at s₀. The lifted point is interior, so the ray interval has positive length. The same is immediate for s₀. Hence the closed support equals the image even if some boundary rays have zero length.

Apply the radial lemma with p=d and the indicator of K. The extended inverse power is the constant one on a convex domain, and the origin need not be in the positive set. On the affine plane (1,s), I_d is exactly the projected density, including value zero on zero-integral rays. The convex gauge therefore gives the extended power −1/d, which is −1/(r+1) in r=d−1. All boundedness, support and positivity hypotheses of the density centerpoint match.

An original homogeneous margin is t(cᵢ+uᵢ·s) at (t,ts). The restrictions cover the entire plane since the original family covers all space. An all-space restriction captures all of K, an empty one captures zero, and the others are proper closed affine halfspaces. One contains the projected center and its density mass equals the original cap volume. The cap lower bound follows without replacing the projective law by uniform projected volume.

At a boundary contact y, let e point to the side containing K. For every ε>0, translating all Hᵢ by −εe keeps the finite cover and places the new contact y−εe strictly outside K. Equivalently the original caps are evaluated on K+εe with unchanged y and unchanged body volume. Off the finitely many original boundary planes the cap indicators converge, and dominated convergence gives individual mass convergence. The finite maximum is continuous, so the exterior lower bound holds at y as well.

For a centroid-zero r-simplex the barycentric coordinate λᵢ has constant term 1/(r+1), and the gradients sum to zero and span the dual of the simplex directions. For any threshold q∈[0,1], the λᵢ≥q cap is qvᵢ+(1−q)T, with fraction (1−q)^r. Its centroid threshold gives γᵣ, including 1/2 for d=2 and 4/9 for d=3. Both sharpness bodies are the part of the cone generated by (1,T) in the respective height ranges, hence compact, convex and full-dimensional. At positive heights the section fraction is constant and the zero-height apex has zero d-volume. The gradients' zero sum gives a whole-space cover, and their span makes the common boundary intersection exactly the t-axis.

Replacing (0,β₀) by (ε,β₀) and (−ε,β₀) and weighting this pair by one and the others by two gives exact zero sum. Their difference produces the t-direction and their sum recovers β₀, proving full rank for each ε>0. The common boundary intersection is y plus the orthogonal complement of the normal span, so full rank is equivalent to uniqueness. On every positive slice the new thresholds are 1/(r+1)−ε and 1/(r+1)+ε. The stated ε cutoff puts both in (0,1), giving fractions (r/(r+1)+ε)^r and (r/(r+1)−ε)^r. The larger is the maximum and tends to γᵣ from above for both bodies. Cross-checked the threshold and fraction formulas in exact rational arithmetic for r=1,…,10 and three positive ε values for each r.

In d=1 proper closed halfspaces through y are the two orientations and a whole-line cover contains both. If y is exterior or an endpoint, the orientation toward K contains all of the interval, so γ₀=1 is attained in both classes. In higher-dimensional normal rank one, whole-space coverage still forces an opposite pair, yielding at least |K|/2 by their two complementary interiors and null common hyperplane. A nominated exterior point can lie in that hyperplane even when it bisects K, so the d=1 full-mass argument cannot be applied from rank one alone.

A positive d-volume fiber of a compact convex body is full-dimensional in its continuous plane. For the given actual common point y, if some restricted normal is zero, the zero margin makes that closed cap contain the fiber in full. Otherwise positive weights summing the margins to zero force a nonnegative margin at every x and hence a whole-plane cover by proper closed halfspaces through y. For y outside the fiber interior the theorem applies on that fiber; every total mixed mass dominates its own fiber contribution, and taking maxima preserves this ordering. A strict budget for every cap in that same subfamily forces y into int K_z. This argument neither compares maximizers across fibers nor requires weights from other contact points.

The planar cover and mixed-fiber ledger allow general open cap covers of each fiber, with the generic maximal cap fraction 4/9. The present result assumes a whole-plane closed cover through one actual exterior or boundary contact and gives 1/2 in the plane.

Its counterexample projects and sums discrete positive-fiber masses from a mixed body and reaches depth below 4/9 in the projected plane. The candidate instead projects ordinary volume over a continuum of heights, with exact t^(d−1) integration. The weighted shadows in that counterexample have no matching inverse-power hypothesis.

The projective proof for affine-exponential and log-concave densities concerns average depth, using different hypotheses and constants. It does not imply a sharp fixed-cover exterior or boundary result.
